Espresso Exposé is an interactive artwork that highlights how Artificial Intelligence is increasingly reshaping our daily lives. Through interaction with a "coffee recommender" agent, the audience encounters the contrast between the direct, front-end results and the opaque, back-end processes of machine learning operations—raising the question: What exactly is happening behind the scenes?

Planet Painter is a desktop program developed in collaboration with the think tank [The Why Factory](https://www.mvrdv.nl/projects/368/the-why-factory) of the Dutch Architecture firm [MVRDV](https://www.mvrdv.nl/themes/15/next) aimed at visualizing and quantifying the impact of different kinds of urban interventions such as replacing cars with trees on the climate. By using satellite imagery, these kinds of scenarios can be generated even for underserved communities for which traditionally not enough data is collected to explore such scenarios.

My thesis (Secure MPC-Sortition: Consolidating Innovations in Democracy and Cryptography) explores how Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) can enhance privacy in citizens’ assembly sortition while maintaining fairness. Two MPC-based designs are proposed: one concealing participant details from organizers and another allowing local governments to contribute encrypted citizen data. I received a 9 out of 10.

If Hobbes had Twitter, he’d be a doomer boomer. My paper, Anxiety in the State of Nature: A Heideggerian Reading of the Leviathan, reexamines Hobbes’ vision of human nature through the lens of existentialist philosophy. I argue that the Hobbesian man’s surrender to despotism is a misguided attempt to escape the existential dread of mortality. Maybe trading freedom for security is just running from the void.

My bachelor thesis (Deconstructing Transformers: Derrida’s Philosophy of Language in the Era of Large Language Models) was no exception in this regard, applying post modernist, anti-rational thinking to LLMs. I received an 8.2 out of 10. The second reader was sadly a rationalist.

Kafka’s _The Trial_ reads like a bureaucratic nightmare, but my essay (_The Failure of Genuine Self-Expression in Kafka’s The Trial_) argues that it’s actually an existential one. Drawing on Camus' notion of the absurd, I examine how K. passively succumbs to his predicament, failing to assert his existential freedom. The real tragedy isn’t just K.’s execution—it’s his failure to revolt, to carve out meaning in a world that denies it.
